2.1.goal: Recognise and write a simple sentence: one subject-verb group that can stand alone.

spot.intro: Tap each sentence to see what makes it simple.

sentences.t: Maya plays tennis.
sentences.label: Simple sentence
sentences.note: One subject (Maya) and one verb (plays).

sentences.t: Maya plays tennis on Saturday mornings at the club.
sentences.label: Still simple
sentences.note: More detail doesn’t change the type. There is still one subject and one verb.

sentences.t: Maya and her sister play tennis.
sentences.label: Still simple
sentences.note: Two subjects share one verb. It is still one idea.

sentences.t: Maya plays tennis and swims.
sentences.label: Still simple
sentences.note: Two verbs share one subject. It is still one idea.

spot.takeaway: A **simple sentence** has **one independent clause**: one subject-verb group that can stand alone. It can be short or long.

practice.q: Which is a simple sentence?
options: Because the bus was late.
The bus was late, so we walked.
The bus arrived late at the station.
practice.why: It has one subject (the bus) and one verb (arrived), and it stands alone.

help.nudge: Count the subject-verb groups. A simple sentence has only one.
help.rule: A **simple sentence** has **one independent clause**: one subject-and-verb group that can stand alone.
help.worked: “The bus arrived late at the station.” has one group (the bus + arrived). “The bus was late, so we walked.” has two (the bus was late / we walked).

options: My uncle repairs old watches in his small shop.
My uncle repairs watches, and his son sells them.
When my uncle repairs watches.
variants.why: One subject-verb group: my uncle repairs.

practice.q: Is each sentence simple or not simple?

items.t: Our team won the match.
Our team won the match, and we celebrated.
The children played in the garden after lunch.
Although it rained, we played outside.

practice.why: A simple sentence has one subject-verb group. The other two have two.

help.nudge: Count the verbs that have their own subject.
help.rule: Simple = **one** subject-verb group.
help.worked: “Our team won the match, and we celebrated.” has two groups: our team won / we celebrated.

practice.q: Make this simple sentence longer by adding where and when. Keep one subject-verb group.
practice.example: The baker works at a small shop every morning.
practice.why: Many answers work. Add details such as where, when or what kind, but don’t add a second subject and verb.

help.nudge: Add where and when, for example “at …” and “every …”.
help.rule: Details (place, time, description) can be added to a simple sentence without changing its type.
help.worked: “The baker works at a small shop every morning.” adds where and when. There is still one subject (the baker) and one verb (works).

variants.q: Make this simple sentence longer by adding where and when. Keep one subject-verb group.
variants.example: The students study in the library after class.
variants.why: Add details, but keep one subject-verb group.

practice.q: Put the words in order to make a simple sentence.
answers: We walked along the river after dinner.
practice.why: One subject (We), one verb (walked), then the details.

help.nudge: Start with who did it.
help.rule: Order: subject, verb, then the details.
help.worked: We (subject) walked (verb) along the river after dinner (details).

practice.q: Which sentence is simple, even though it is long?
options: Every Friday evening my parents visit my grandmother in the old part of the city.
My parents visit my grandmother, and they bring her fruit.
My parents visit my grandmother because she lives alone.
practice.why: It has only one subject-verb group (my parents visit). The other two have two.

help.nudge: Length doesn’t matter. Count the subject-verb groups.
help.rule: A long sentence can still be simple if it has only one subject-verb group.
help.worked: Option 1: my parents visit. Option 2: my parents visit + they bring. Option 3: my parents visit + she lives.

write.prompt: Write **two simple sentences** about your neighbourhood. Add details, but keep one subject-verb group in each.

checks.t: Each sentence has one subject-verb group (details are fine).
I added details (where, when or what kind).
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: My neighbourhood has a small park near the school. Children play football there after lessons.

2.2.goal: Join two subjects or two verbs inside one simple sentence.

spot.intro: Tap each sentence to see what is joined.

sentences.t: Sara and Omar study together.
sentences.label: Compound subject
sentences.note: Two subjects, one verb. The verb is plural: study.

sentences.t: Sara studies at night and works in the morning.
sentences.label: Compound verb
sentences.note: One subject, two verbs. No comma is needed.

sentences.t: My mother and my aunt cook and serve the food.
sentences.label: Both together
sentences.note: Two subjects and two verbs. It is still one clause, so it is still simple.

spot.takeaway: Join subjects or verbs with **and** or **or**. It is still one clause, so you don’t need a comma.

practice.q: Tap the two subjects.
practice.text: Hamad and Ali play football every Friday.
practice.why: “Hamad” and “Ali” are the two subjects. They share the verb “play”.

help.nudge: Who plays football? There are two answers.
help.rule: A **compound subject** is two (or more) subjects joined by and / or.
help.worked: Hamad and Ali are both doing the action, so both are subjects.

variants.text: Layla and her cousin visit the museum on Sundays.

practice.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: Rana and her cousin studies English.
Rana and her cousin study English.
Rana and her cousin is studying English.
practice.why: Two subjects joined by “and” need a plural verb: study.

help.nudge: Is the subject one person, or more than one?
help.rule: Compound subject with **and** → plural verb: study, are, have.
help.worked: Rana + her cousin = two people, so the verb is “study” (not “studies”).

options: Ali and Hamad plays chess.
Ali and Hamad play chess.
Ali and Hamad is playing chess.
variants.why: Two subjects with “and” take a plural verb.

practice.q: Combine the two sentences into one with a compound verb. No comma.
practice.show: Lina cooks dinner. Lina washes the dishes.
accept: Lina cooks dinner and washes the dishes.
Lina cooks dinner and then washes the dishes.
practice.example: Lina cooks dinner and washes the dishes.
practice.why: Both verbs share one subject, so join them with “and”. You don’t repeat “Lina”.

help.nudge: Say “Lina” only once, then join the two actions with and.
help.rule: A **compound verb** is one subject with two verbs joined by and / or.
help.worked: Lina cooks dinner and washes the dishes.

variants.q: Combine the two sentences into one with a compound verb. No comma.
variants.show: Karim opens the shop. Karim sells fruit.
accept: Karim opens the shop and sells fruit.
variants.example: Karim opens the shop and sells fruit.
variants.why: One subject, two verbs joined by and.

practice.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Sara studies at night, and works in the morning.
Sara studies at night and works in the morning.
Sara studies at night; and works in the morning.
practice.why: A compound verb is not a new clause, so there is no comma.

help.nudge: Does “works in the morning” have its own subject?
help.rule: No comma between two verbs that share one subject.
help.worked: “works in the morning” has no new subject, so it is not a separate clause. No comma is needed.

practice.q: Combine the two sentences into one with a compound subject.
practice.show: Omar likes tea. Fatima likes tea.
practice.why: Join the subjects with “and”. The verb changes to “like”.

help.nudge: Join the two names, then say the verb once. Does the verb change?
help.rule: Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb (like, not likes).
help.worked: Omar and Fatima like tea.

variants.q: Combine the two sentences into one with a compound subject.
variants.show: Ali plays chess. Hamad plays chess.

write.prompt: Write **two sentences** about you and a friend or family member: one with a compound subject and one with a compound verb.

checks.t: One sentence has two subjects joined by and / or.
One sentence has two verbs joined by and / or, with no comma.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: My sister and I walk to school together. We talk and laugh all the way.

2.3.goal: Join two complete sentences with a comma and a FANBOYS word.

sentences.t: The shop was closed, so we went home.
sentences.label: so = result
sentences.note: Two complete sentences joined by a comma + so.

sentences.t: I like tea, but my brother prefers coffee.
sentences.label: but = contrast
sentences.note: But shows a contrast.

sentences.t: You can take the bus, or you can walk.
sentences.label: or = choice
sentences.note: Or offers a choice.

sentences.t: She was ill, yet she came to class.
sentences.label: yet = surprise
sentences.note: Yet shows something unexpected.

spot.takeaway: A **compound sentence** = complete sentence + **comma** + **FANBOYS word** + complete sentence.

practice.q: Which is a correct compound sentence?
options: I wanted to go, but it was too late.
I wanted to go but, it was too late.
I wanted to go, it was too late.
practice.why: A comma comes before the joining word, and both parts are complete sentences.

help.nudge: Where does the comma go: before or after the joining word?
help.rule: **Clause + comma + FANBOYS + clause.** The comma comes before the joining word.
help.worked: “I wanted to go” + , + but + “it was too late”.

variants.q: Which is a correct compound sentence?
options: The film was long, yet we enjoyed it.
The film was long yet, we enjoyed it.
The film was long, we enjoyed it.
variants.why: Comma before “yet”, and both parts are complete.

practice.q: Choose the best joining word: “The test was difficult, ___ I passed it.”
options: so
but
or
practice.why: “But” shows a contrast: it was difficult, yet I passed.

help.nudge: Is the second part a result, or a surprise?
help.rule: **so** = result · **but / yet** = contrast · **or** = choice · **and** = addition.
help.worked: Passing a difficult test is a surprise, so we use “but” (or “yet”).

practice.q: Join the sentences with a comma and a joining word.
practice.show: It was late. We kept walking.
practice.example: It was late, but we kept walking.
practice.why: Several joining words work: but and yet show contrast, and adds, so shows a result.

help.nudge: Put a comma after “late”, then choose a joining word.
help.rule: **Clause + comma + FANBOYS + clause.**
help.worked: It was late, but we kept walking.

variants.q: Join the sentences with a comma and a joining word.
variants.show: The bus was full. We waited for the next one.
patterns: ^The bus was full, (so|and) we waited for the next one\.$
variants.example: The bus was full, so we waited for the next one.
variants.why: So shows the result; and also works.

practice.q: Add the missing comma.
practice.show: She likes coffee but he prefers tea.
accept: She likes coffee, but he prefers tea.
practice.example: She likes coffee, but he prefers tea.
practice.why: A compound sentence needs a comma before the joining word.

help.nudge: Find the joining word. The comma goes just before it.
help.rule: Put the comma **before** the FANBOYS word.
help.worked: She likes coffee, but he prefers tea.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
answers: We could take a taxi, or we could walk.
practice.why: Two complete sentences, joined by a comma and “or”.

help.nudge: Which word joins the two parts? The comma comes right before it.
help.rule: **Clause + comma + FANBOYS + clause.**
help.worked: We could take a taxi, or we could walk.

write.prompt: Write **two compound sentences** about plans for this weekend. Use a comma and a joining word (so, but, or, yet…) in each.

checks.t: Each half could stand alone as a sentence.
I used a comma before the joining word.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: I want to visit the beach, but the weather may be cold. We could go to the cinema, or we could stay home.

2.4.goal: Join two closely related complete sentences with a semicolon.

spot.intro: A semicolon works like a full stop that keeps two ideas close. Tap each sentence.

sentences.t: The library closes at nine; students must leave by then.
sentences.label: Semicolon
sentences.note: It joins two complete sentences that are closely related.

sentences.t: She loves music; her brother prefers sports.
sentences.label: No joining word
sentences.note: No and / but / so is needed after the semicolon.

sentences.t: The soup was cold; I ordered another one.
sentences.label: Cause and result
sentences.note: Both sides could stand alone as sentences.

spot.takeaway: **Complete sentence ; complete sentence.** Use it instead of a full stop for two closely linked ideas. Don’t add and / but / so after it.

practice.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: The bus was late; we walked home.
The bus was late; so we walked home.
The bus; was late, we walked.
practice.why: Both sides are complete sentences, and there is no joining word after the semicolon.

help.nudge: Can both sides stand alone? And is there a joining word after the semicolon?
help.rule: **Complete sentence ; complete sentence.** No and / but / so right after it.
help.worked: “The bus was late” and “we walked home” are both complete, so the semicolon works. In option 2, “so” should not follow it.

variants.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: It rained all morning; the match was cancelled.
It rained all morning; and the match was cancelled.
It rained; all morning the match, was cancelled.
variants.why: Two complete sentences, no joining word after the semicolon.

practice.q: Is the semicolon correct?

items.t: I like tea; my sister likes coffee.
I like tea; and my sister likes coffee.
Because I was tired; I slept.
The shop opens at nine; it closes at six.

practice.why: Both sides must be complete sentences, with no joining word after the semicolon.

help.nudge: Check both sides: can each stand alone? Is there a joining word?
help.rule: A semicolon needs a **complete sentence on both sides**, and no and / but / so after it.
help.worked: “Because I was tired” can’t stand alone, so a semicolon is wrong there.

practice.q: Join the sentences with a semicolon instead of a full stop.
practice.show: The museum is free. Everyone is welcome.
accept: The museum is free; everyone is welcome.
practice.example: The museum is free; everyone is welcome.
practice.why: After a semicolon, the next word starts with a small letter (unless it is a name).

help.nudge: Replace the full stop with a semicolon, and use a small letter after it.
help.rule: Semicolon, then a small letter (unless a name).
help.worked: The museum is free; everyone is welcome.

variants.q: Join the sentences with a semicolon instead of a full stop.
variants.show: The park closes at six. Everyone must leave.
accept: The park closes at six; everyone must leave.
variants.example: The park closes at six; everyone must leave.

practice.q: Fix this comma splice with a semicolon.
practice.show: The soup was cold, I ordered another one.
accept: The soup was cold; I ordered another one.
practice.example: The soup was cold; I ordered another one.
practice.why: A comma alone can’t join two sentences. A semicolon can.

help.nudge: Change the comma into a semicolon.
help.rule: A semicolon can fix a comma splice between two complete sentences.
help.worked: The soup was cold; I ordered another one.

practice.q: Which is NOT a good place for a semicolon?
options: The rain stopped; we went outside.
Because I was late; I ran.
My phone broke; I need a new one.
practice.why: “Because I was late” can’t stand alone, so a semicolon can’t follow it.

help.nudge: Can “Because I was late” stand alone as a sentence?
help.rule: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides.
help.worked: “Because I was late” is a subordinate clause. A comma would work: “Because I was late, I ran.”

write.prompt: Write **two sentences** about your day. Use a semicolon to join two related ideas in each.

checks.t: Both sides of each semicolon are complete sentences.
I did not use and / but / so right after the semicolon.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: I woke up early; the city was still quiet. My class starts at nine; I never want to be late.

2.5.goal: Recognise a subordinate clause: it has a subject and a verb, but it can’t stand alone.

spot.intro: The highlighted part of each sentence is a subordinate clause. Tap to see why.

sentences.t: I stayed home ==because it was raining==.
sentences.label: Subordinate clause
sentences.note: It has a subject (it) and a verb (was), but “because it was raining” can’t stand alone.

sentences.t: ==Although the exam was difficult==, most students passed.
sentences.label: Starts with although
sentences.note: A subordinate clause starts with a word like although.

sentences.t: ==When the bell rang==, the students left.
sentences.label: Starts with when
sentences.note: When, if, because and while work the same way.

sentences.t: ==If you study every day==, you will improve.
sentences.label: Starts with if
sentences.note: Without the main clause, “If you study every day” feels unfinished.

spot.takeaway: A **subordinate clause** has a subject and a verb but **cannot stand alone**. It begins with a word like **because, although, when, if, while, since, after, before**.

practice.q: Can it stand alone as a sentence?

items.t: The road was closed.
Because the road was closed
When we arrived
We arrived late.

practice.why: Words like because and when make a clause need more.

help.nudge: Read it aloud. Does it feel finished?
help.rule: A subordinate clause starts with a word like because / when / although and feels unfinished.
help.worked: “Because the road was closed” leaves us asking “what happened?”, so it can’t stand alone.

practice.q: Tap the subordinate clause (the part that cannot stand alone).
practice.text: We missed the bus because we woke up late.
practice.why: “because we woke up late” can’t stand alone.

help.nudge: Look for the word “because”. The clause starts there.
help.rule: The subordinate clause starts with the subordinating word and runs to the end of that idea.
help.worked: “We missed the bus” can stand alone. “because we woke up late” cannot.

variants.q: Tap the subordinate clause (the part that cannot stand alone).
variants.text: Our flight was delayed because the weather was bad.
variants.why: “because the weather was bad” can’t stand alone.

practice.q: Which word starts a subordinate clause?
options: and
although
but
practice.why: Although, because, when and if start subordinate clauses. And and but are FANBOYS joining words.

help.nudge: Which one is NOT a FANBOYS word?
help.rule: FANBOYS words join equal parts. Words like although start a subordinate clause.
help.worked: “and” and “but” are both in FANBOYS. “although” is not.

practice.q: Fix this fragment by adding a main clause.
practice.example: Although it was cold, we played outside.
practice.why: Many answers work. Add a main clause that can stand alone.

help.nudge: What happened even though it was cold?
help.rule: Fix a subordinate-clause fragment by adding a main clause.
help.worked: Although it was cold, we played outside.

variants.q: Fix this fragment by adding a main clause.
variants.example: Because the shop was closed, we went home.
variants.why: Add a main clause that can stand alone.

practice.q: Which one is a complete sentence?
options: When the lesson finished.
When the lesson finished, we left.
When the lesson finished and.
practice.why: It has a main clause (we left) as well as the subordinate clause.

help.nudge: Which option answers: what happened when the lesson finished?
help.rule: A complete sentence needs a main clause.
help.worked: “we left” is the main clause. The other two only have the “When…” part.

write.prompt: Write **one sentence** with a subordinate clause (start it with because, when, although or if) and a main clause.

checks.t: My sentence has a part that can’t stand alone (the subordinate clause).
It also has a main clause that can stand alone.
It starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: When I finish my homework, I watch a film.

2.6.goal: Write complex sentences and punctuate them correctly.

spot.intro: Watch where the comma goes. Tap each sentence.

sentences.t: ==Because it was raining==, we stayed home.
sentences.label: Subordinate clause first
sentences.note: A comma goes after the opening clause.

sentences.t: We stayed home ==because it was raining==.
sentences.label: Subordinate clause second
sentences.note: Usually no comma.

sentences.t: ==Although he was tired==, he finished the report.
sentences.label: Comma after the although-clause
sentences.note: The clause comes first, so there is a comma.

sentences.t: He finished the report ==although he was tired==.
sentences.label: No comma
sentences.note: Same meaning, clause second, no comma.

spot.takeaway: A **complex sentence** = main clause + subordinate clause. **Subordinate clause first? Add a comma. Second? Usually no comma.**

practice.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: When the class ended we went home.
When the class ended, we went home.
When the class ended; we went home.
practice.why: A comma follows the opening subordinate clause.

help.nudge: The sentence starts with a subordinate clause. What comes after it?
help.rule: Subordinate clause **first** → add a comma.
help.worked: “When the class ended” is the opening clause, so add a comma after it.

options: If you practise every day you will improve.
If you practise every day, you will improve.
If you practise every day; you will improve.

practice.q: Does the sentence need a comma?

items.t: Because I was hungry I ate a sandwich.
I ate a sandwich because I was hungry.
Although it was late we kept working.
We kept working although it was late.

practice.why: A comma is needed only when the subordinate clause comes first.

help.nudge: Which part comes first: the main clause or the subordinate clause?
help.rule: Subordinate clause first → comma. Second → usually no comma.
help.worked: “Because I was hungry” opens the first sentence, so it needs a comma after it.

practice.q: Join the sentences with because. Start with the because-part.
practice.show: We stayed inside. It was cold.
accept: Because it was cold, we stayed inside.
practice.example: Because it was cold, we stayed inside.
practice.why: The because-part comes first, so a comma follows it.

help.nudge: Start with “Because it was cold” and finish with a comma.
help.rule: Opening subordinate clause + comma + main clause.
help.worked: Because it was cold, we stayed inside.

variants.q: Join the sentences with because. Start with the because-part.
variants.show: We took an umbrella. It was raining.
accept: Because it was raining, we took an umbrella.
variants.example: Because it was raining, we took an umbrella.

practice.q: Join the sentences with although.
practice.show: The film was long. I enjoyed it.
accept: Although the film was long, I enjoyed it.
I enjoyed it although the film was long.
practice.example: Although the film was long, I enjoyed it.
practice.why: Both orders are correct. Use a comma only when although comes first.

help.nudge: Start with “Although the film was long”, then add the main clause.
help.rule: Although-clause first → comma. Although-clause second → no comma.
help.worked: Although the film was long, I enjoyed it.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
answers: After we finished dinner, we watched a film.
practice.why: Subordinate clause first, then a comma, then the main clause.

help.nudge: Which clause starts with “After”? A comma follows it.
help.rule: Opening clause + comma + main clause.
help.worked: After we finished dinner, we watched a film.

write.prompt: Write **two complex sentences** about your study habits: start one with the subordinate clause and end the other with it.

checks.t: One sentence starts with a subordinate clause and has a comma after it.
One sentence ends with a subordinate clause and has no comma before it.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: Because I have exams soon, I study every evening. I stay focused when I turn off my phone.

2.7.goal: Recognise a sentence with two main clauses and a subordinate clause. This lesson is optional.

spot.intro: An optional stretch lesson. Tap each sentence.

sentences.t: ==Although it was late==, we kept working, and we finished the report.
sentences.label: Compound-complex
sentences.note: Two main clauses (we kept working / we finished the report) and one subordinate clause (Although it was late).

sentences.t: We waited ==because the train was late==, but it never came.
sentences.label: Compound-complex
sentences.note: A main clause with a subordinate clause, joined by “but” to a second main clause.

sentences.t: I like tea, but my brother likes coffee.
sentences.label: Only compound
sentences.note: There is no subordinate clause here, so this is compound, not compound-complex.

spot.takeaway: **Compound-complex** = two or more main clauses + at least one subordinate clause. It is a bonus skill: use these sentences sparingly.

practice.q: What type is each sentence?

items.t: We walked.
The bus was late, so we walked.
Because the bus was late, we walked.
Because the bus was late, we walked, and we arrived after the lesson began.

practice.why: Count the main clauses and the subordinate clauses.

help.nudge: Count the main clauses, then the subordinate clauses.
help.rule: Simple: 1 main. Compound: 2+ main. Complex: 1 main + 1+ subordinate. Compound-complex: 2+ main + 1+ subordinate.
help.worked: The last sentence has two main clauses (we walked / we arrived…) and one subordinate clause (Because the bus was late).

practice.q: Which sentence is compound-complex?
options: We waited because the train was late, but it never came.
We waited, and it never came.
We waited until it came.
practice.why: Two main clauses (we waited / it never came) and one subordinate clause (because the train was late).

help.nudge: Look for two main clauses AND one subordinate clause.
help.rule: Compound-complex needs both: 2+ main clauses and 1+ subordinate clause.
help.worked: Option 2 has two main clauses only (compound). Option 3 has one main and one subordinate (complex).

practice.q: Join the three ideas into one sentence. Use a because / when / while part and a comma + and.
practice.show: It was raining. We stayed inside. We watched a film.
patterns: ^(Because|Since|As|When|While) it was raining, we stayed inside,? (and|so) we watched a film\.$
^We stayed inside (because|since|as) it was raining,? (and|so) we watched a film\.$
practice.example: Because it was raining, we stayed inside, and we watched a film.
practice.why: Many orders work. You need one subordinate clause and two main clauses.

help.nudge: Which idea is the reason? Make that the subordinate clause.
help.rule: Reason → subordinate clause. Two actions → two main clauses joined by a comma and “and”.
help.worked: Because it was raining (subordinate), we stayed inside (main), and we watched a film (main).

practice.q: How should you use compound-complex sentences?
options: Everywhere: longer sentences are always better.
Sparingly: mix them with shorter sentences so your writing stays clear.
Never: they are always wrong.
practice.why: Long sentences can be powerful but hard to read. Variety is the goal.

help.nudge: Think about your reader.
help.rule: Clear writing mixes sentence types and lengths.
help.worked: Too many long sentences tire the reader; a few, among shorter ones, work well.

write.prompt: (Optional) Write **one compound-complex sentence** about a busy day.

checks.t: It has two main clauses.
It has a subordinate clause (because, although, when…).
It starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

focus: Shorten it if it is too long
write.sample: Although I was tired, I finished my homework, and I helped my sister with hers.

2.8.goal: Mix short and long sentences and different sentence types so your writing flows.

spot.intro: Same ideas, different rhythm. Tap each sentence.

sentences.t: I woke up. I ate breakfast. I went to school. I met my friends.
sentences.label: Choppy
sentences.note: Four short simple sentences in a row. It sounds repetitive.

sentences.t: After I woke up, I ate breakfast and went to school, where I met my friends.
sentences.label: Varied
sentences.note: The same ideas, joined smoothly into one sentence.

sentences.t: I woke up late; I ate quickly.
sentences.label: A semicolon for variety
sentences.note: A semicolon can link two short, related ideas.

sentences.t: It worked.
sentences.label: Short for emphasis
sentences.note: A very short sentence after longer ones adds emphasis.

spot.takeaway: Mix **short and long** sentences, and **simple, compound and complex** types. Don’t make every sentence the same shape.

practice.q: Which version reads best?
options: We arrived. We checked in. We ate dinner. We went to bed.
After we arrived and checked in, we ate dinner and went to bed.
We arrived and we checked in and we ate dinner and we went to bed.
practice.why: Option 2 combines the ideas smoothly. Option 1 is choppy; option 3 repeats “we … and”.

help.nudge: Which version sounds smoothest when you read it aloud?
help.rule: Combine short sentences with a subordinate clause or a compound verb.
help.worked: “After we arrived and checked in” (opening clause), then “ate dinner and went to bed” (compound verb).

options: I got home. I made tea. I read a book.
After I got home, I made tea and read a book.
I got home and I made tea and I read a book.

practice.q: Combine the three sentences into ONE smoother sentence.
practice.show: I finished work. I went to the gym. I felt energetic.
practice.example: After I finished work, I went to the gym, and I felt energetic.
practice.why: Many answers work. Use and, because or after to join all three ideas in one sentence.

help.nudge: Pick one idea to open the sentence (for example “After I finished work…”) and join the rest.
help.rule: Use a subordinate clause, a compound verb or a joining word to combine ideas.
help.worked: After I finished work, I went to the gym and felt energetic.

variants.q: Combine the three sentences into ONE smoother sentence.
variants.show: It was late. I was hungry. I made dinner.
variants.example: Because it was late and I was hungry, I made dinner.
variants.why: Join all three ideas in one sentence.

practice.q: After two long sentences, which sentence adds emphasis?
options: It was a very big success for everyone who took part in the project.
It worked.
The project which we started in January was successful.
practice.why: A very short sentence stands out after longer ones.

help.nudge: Which sentence is the shortest and punchiest?
help.rule: A short sentence after longer ones adds emphasis.
help.worked: “It worked.” is only two words, so it stands out.

practice.q: Which type is each sentence?

items.t: We left early.
We left early, but the road was still busy.
We left early because the road is usually busy.
The road was busy.

practice.why: Simple: one group. Compound: two main clauses. Complex: a main clause and a subordinate clause.

help.nudge: Look for a FANBOYS word (compound) or a word like because (complex).
help.rule: Simple: 1 clause. Compound: clause, FANBOYS, clause. Complex: main clause + subordinate clause.
help.worked: “…, but the road was still busy” uses but (compound). “…because the road is usually busy” uses because (complex).

practice.q: Rewrite the three sentences as one sentence in your own way.
practice.show: I was tired. I had homework. I stayed up late.
practice.example: Although I was tired, I had homework, so I stayed up late.
practice.why: Many answers work. Join all three ideas with a linking word or clause.

help.nudge: Which idea is the surprise or the reason? Use although or because for it.
help.rule: Combine with a subordinate clause and a joining word.
help.worked: Although I was tired, I had homework, so I stayed up late.

write.prompt: Rewrite this choppy paragraph in your own words, mixing sentence types: **I woke up. I made tea. I read the news. I went to work.**

checks.t: I joined some ideas (not all short sentences in a row).
I used at least two different sentence types.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: After I woke up, I made tea and read the news. Then I went to work.

2.9.goal: Show that you can recognise and use simple, compound and complex sentences.

write.prompt: Write a short paragraph (4–5 sentences) about your favourite place. Use at least one **compound** sentence and one **complex** sentence.

checks.t: I wrote a compound sentence: a comma and a joining word.
I wrote a complex sentence with the right comma, and my sentences are not all the same length.
Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation.

write.sample: My favourite place is the old market in the city centre. It is crowded, but I love the colours and the smells. When I visit, I always buy fresh bread. The sellers know me, so they often give me a small gift.

simple.label: Simple sentences
simple.good: You can spot a simple sentence.
simple.improve: A simple sentence has one subject-verb group, however long it is.

cv.label: Compound subjects and verbs
cv.good: You join subjects and verbs well.
cv.improve: Join two subjects or two verbs with and / or, and use no comma.

fanboys.label: Joining with FANBOYS
fanboys.good: You join sentences with a comma and a joining word.

semi.label: Semicolons
semi.improve: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides and no and / but / so after it.

subclause.label: Subordinate clauses
subclause.improve: A subordinate clause starts with because, although, when, if… and can’t stand alone.

complex.label: Complex sentences
complex.improve: Subordinate clause first? Add a comma. Second? Usually no comma.

cc.label: Compound-complex sentences
cc.improve: Compound-complex = two main clauses + a subordinate clause.

variety.label: Sentence variety
variety.improve: Mix short and long sentences and different types.
